learn: FITT stands for Frequency (how often), Intensity (how hard), Time (how long) and Type (what activity).
Adjusting FITT helps you improve fitness safely.
Example: jog (type) 3 days a week (frequency) at moderate effort (intensity) for 20 minutes (time).
check: The I in FITT stands for...
"Jogging" in a FITT plan is the...
lessons.try: Write a FITT plan for one week.

learn: To improve, gradually increase the challenge: more reps, longer time or harder intensity.
Increase slowly, about 10% a week, to avoid injury.
Rest days let muscles rebuild stronger.
lessons.try: Track push-ups for three weeks, adding one or two each week.

learn: Children aged 6-17 need at least 60 minutes of moderate-to-vigorous activity daily.
Include muscle-strengthening and bone-strengthening activity at least 3 days a week.
Limit sitting time and take movement breaks.
check: Children need at least ___ minutes of activity daily.
Muscle strengthening should happen at least...
lessons.try: Log your activity minutes for a week.

learn: A rough estimate of maximum heart rate is 220 minus your age.
For a 10-year-old, that's about 210 beats per minute.
A target zone for vigorous exercise is about 60-85% of maximum.
check: For a 10-year-old, estimated max is about...
A vigorous target zone is about ___ of max.
lessons.try: Calculate your estimated maximum and target zone.

learn: Use pulse checks, the talk test, or a scale of perceived exertion (1-10).
Moderate is about 5-6 on the scale; vigorous is 7-8.
Heart rate monitors and fitness watches can track intensity.
check: Vigorous effort is about ___ on a 1-10 scale.
lessons.try: Rate your effort 1-10 during three different activities.

learn: SMART goals are Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant and Time-bound.
"Run a mile in under 10 minutes by June" is SMART.
Review goals regularly and celebrate progress.
check: Run a mile under 10 minutes by June
lessons.try: Write a SMART goal for the next six weeks.

units.t: Sports Skills: Striking, Kicking and Volleying

learn: Stand sideways, feet shoulder-width apart, bat back and elbows up.
Step toward the pitch, rotate hips and swing level.
Keep your eye on the ball until contact and follow through.
lessons.try: Hit balls off a tee 20 times focusing on hip rotation.

learn: A punt drops the ball and kicks it before it touches the ground.
Contact with the top of the foot (laces) and keep your toe pointed.
Follow through upward for height.
lessons.try: Punt a soft ball ten times for distance.

learn: The forearm pass (bump) uses a flat platform of forearms.
The overhead set uses fingertips forming a triangle above the forehead.
The overhand serve uses a toss and a firm hit with the heel of the hand.
check: An overhand serve hits with the...
lessons.try: Practise 20 bumps and 20 sets against a wall.

learn: Rules keep games fair and safe.
Officials enforce rules; players respect their calls.
Knowing the rules helps you play smarter.
lessons.try: Explain the main rules of a sport to someone who doesn't know it.

learn: Offensive tactics: create space, move without the ball, pass quickly.
Defensive tactics: mark opponents, stay between them and the goal, communicate.
Transition is switching quickly between offence and defence.
check: Switching between offence and defence is...
lessons.try: Draw a play for a small-sided game.

learn: Captains lead by example: effort, positivity and fairness.
Respect teammates, opponents, officials and equipment.
Handle conflict calmly and seek solutions.
lessons.try: Lead a warm-up for a group, encouraging everyone.

learn: Carbohydrates are the main fuel for activity; choose whole grains, fruits and vegetables.
Proteins repair and build tissues: beans, eggs, fish, meat, nuts and dairy.
Fats help absorb vitamins; choose healthy fats like nuts, seeds and olive oil.
check: The main fuel for activity is...
lessons.try: Label each food on your dinner plate by its main macronutrient.

learn: Vitamins and minerals are needed in small amounts: vitamin C helps healing; iron carries oxygen in blood.
Calcium and vitamin D build strong bones.
Fibre aids digestion and is found in whole grains, beans, fruits and vegetables.
lessons.try: Find foods rich in vitamin C, iron and calcium.

learn: Eat a balanced meal 2-3 hours before activity, or a light snack 30-60 minutes before.
Drink water before, during and after exercise.
After exercise, refuel with carbohydrates and protein.
check: A balanced meal should be eaten about ___ before activity.
When should you drink water around exercise?
lessons.try: Plan a pre-game snack and a post-game meal.

learn: The circulatory system (heart, blood vessels) moves blood. The respiratory system (lungs) brings in oxygen.
The skeletal system supports the body; the muscular system moves it.
The nervous system controls everything; the digestive system processes food.
lessons.try: Make a chart of five body systems and their main organs.

learn: Puberty is when the body develops from a child's into an adult's, triggered by hormones.
Changes include growth spurts, body hair, voice changes and skin changes; timing differs for everyone.
Emotions can feel stronger during puberty; this is normal.
check: Do all people start puberty at the same time?
lessons.try: Write down a question about growing up to ask a parent, nurse or school counsellor.

learn: Shower daily, use deodorant, and wash your face to help with acne.
Wear clean clothes and get enough sleep.
Ask trusted adults or a doctor about any concerns.
check: Washing your face can help with...
Who can you ask about body changes?
lessons.try: Create a personal care checklist.

learn: Children aged 6-12 need 9-12 hours of sleep each night.
Sleep helps memory, growth, mood and the immune system.
Lack of sleep hurts focus and performance.
lessons.try: Track your sleep for one week.

learn: Keep a regular bedtime and wake time, even on weekends.
Avoid caffeine and screens before bed.
Keep your room cool, dark and quiet.
check: The best bedroom for sleep is...
lessons.try: Design an ideal bedtime routine.

learn: Too much screen time can reduce sleep, activity and face-to-face time.
Set limits and choose quality content.
Take breaks: every 20 minutes, look 20 feet away for 20 seconds (20-20-20 rule).
check: Too much screen time can reduce...
lessons.try: Make a family media plan.

learn: Check the scene for danger, then check the person.
Call 911 for serious emergencies and give your location clearly.
Don't move an injured person unless they are in danger.
check: Should you move an injured person?
lessons.try: Role-play a 911 call with a family member.

learn: For sprains, use RICE: Rest, Ice, Compression, Elevation.
For minor burns, cool under running water for 10-20 minutes; never use butter or ice.
For bleeding, apply firm pressure with a clean cloth.
check: RICE stands for Rest, Ice, Compression and...
lessons.try: Practise wrapping a pretend sprained ankle.

learn: Wear the right gear: helmets, mouth guards, shin guards and proper shoes.
Report concussion symptoms like headache, dizziness or confusion; stop playing.
Never play through pain; tell a coach or adult.
check: After a head injury with dizziness, you should...
Stop playing and tell an adult
lessons.try: Make a safety gear checklist for your favourite sport.

learn: Personal information includes your full name, address, school, phone number, passwords and photos.
Use strong passwords and never share them except with parents.
Check privacy settings on apps and games.
lessons.try: Create a strong password example (don't use it) with letters, numbers and symbols.

learn: Your digital footprint is the trail of everything you post or do online.
Posts can be permanent, even if deleted.
Think before you post: Is it true? Is it kind? Would I want everyone to see it?
lessons.try: Write three questions to ask yourself before posting.

learn: Cyberbullying is bullying through devices: mean messages, rumours or exclusion online.
Don't respond; save evidence; block the person; tell a trusted adult.
Be an upstander online: support targets and report bullying.
check: Save evidence and tell an adult
lessons.try: Write a pledge for kind online behaviour.

learn: Recognising your emotions is the first step to managing them.
Physical signals, like a racing heart or tight muscles, can show stress or anger.
Naming emotions precisely (frustrated, disappointed, anxious) helps you respond well.
check: The first step to managing emotions is...
lessons.try: Make a list of 15 emotion words.

learn: Resilience is bouncing back from setbacks.
Healthy coping includes exercise, journaling, talking to someone, mindfulness and hobbies.
Mistakes are chances to learn: a "growth mindset".
check: A growth mindset sees mistakes as...
lessons.try: Write about a setback you overcame.

learn: Healthy relationships have respect, trust, honesty and good communication.
Unhealthy signs include pressure, control, put-downs and not respecting boundaries.
Use "I" statements to communicate: "I feel hurt when..."
lessons.try: Practise three "I" statements.
